title: Powerful Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast as beachside communities and tourist areas prepare for impacts | CNN
text:
Lee el artículo en español

Source: CNN

Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.

The international airport in Puerto Vallarta, a resort city on the shore of Bahía de Banderas, suspended operations as the powerful storm moved north-northwest offshore, along the coast of Mexico.

Initial models projected Simon would make landfall as a Category 4 storm Sunday, but its path has shifted and is getting harder to predict. The storm weakened to a Category 3 Sunday night and is now expected to remain offshore through Monday though models are split on whether it will move inland or stay entirely offshore.

The hurricane is moving at a speed of 5 mph with maximum winds of 120 mph, according to the 11 p.m. ETreportissued Sunday by the US National Hurricane Center (NHC).

“Simon moving slowly just offshore of west-central Mexico… threat of destructive winds and flooding rains continues along the coast,” the NHC report said.

The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.”

But authorities are urging residents to take shelter, as the storm’s path is still somewhat uncertain.

“We ask that you remain vigilant,” Velázquez said.

The coordinator said that the effects of Simon — which include “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday.

The storm’s current projected path indicates that it has several “probable impacts” on certain states, which is why “Simon concerns us greatly,” Dr. Jorge Zavala, a climate scientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, told CNN.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaumurgedresidents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states.

“The wind and rain will suddenly and deceptively subside, creating an apparent calm that does not mean the danger has passed,” the agency warned in a statement.

Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday.

Along the boardwalk in Puerto Vallarta, police reminded tourists that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter as the storm approaches, the Associated Press reported.

“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” visitor Brenda Villareal told the AP. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”

Mexico’s Navydeployedmore than 4,600 personnel to help with the response to the incoming storm, along with excavation equipment, heavy machinery, and other emergency resources.

As Simon moves closer to the coast,its heavy rain has already caused damage.

Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis.

In Manzanillo, the Navy helped remove water from some houses that were flooded by the storm.

Manzanillo resident Cecilia Palomar told Reuters that the water started rising in her home at dawn.

“It had risen before, but not like this,” Palomar said. “Beds, refrigerators, heaters, all the furniture got wet, the whole house is flooded.”

The Pacific Airport Group (GAP) reported that the Puerto Vallarta airport will remain closed until 10 a.m. ET on Monday. Flights at the airport in Manzanillo were also suspended for the day.

Laura Sharman and Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.
